gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the MacBook Neo, Apple's A18 Pro student-priced MacBook, sends video from only one of its two USB-C ports (the USB 3 port; the other is USB 2 with no DisplayPort) and drives one external display, so on a Neo a dual-screen extender extends at most one added screen without a driver, and Thunderbolt-only devices do not work at all.
standout_why: I compared against three pages. Macworld's best portable monitors for Mac (cited, 2026-10-16) does say that plain M1/M2 Macs 'plus the new MacBook Neo are limited to connecting just a single monitor', but only in its Trio 3 Pro entry. It does not say which Neo port carries video, that the second port is USB 2 with no DisplayPort, or that Thunderbolt-only devices are excluded. iTechGuides' 15 best laptop screen extenders for 2026 (cited) says only that Mac compatibility depends on the 'Intel or Apple silicon generation' and gives no limits for each chip. ChatGPT's own answer says only 'check whether your MacBook supports an additional external display'. TechRepublic (cited) returned HTTP 403 and I could not compare it. So part of the finding is already on a cited page and part is new. That is why the score is 1.
decides: For a student on a MacBook Neo, the finding points the pick to a single added screen: a Duex DS-series slide-out or a freestanding 14-inch monitor, plugged into the Neo's USB 3 port. Dual extenders like the FOPO S1 or S7 only give two extended screens on a Neo through a driver. The Trio 3 Pro is in the same position: Macworld says it needs Mobile Pixels' free software on the Neo. On the current M5 MacBook Air (two Thunderbolt 4 ports, two external displays) a driver-free dual extender stays a valid pick. So the page should split its pick by laptop. The FOPO S1 and S7 rows still need FOPO's own wording on how they behave on Macs that drive one external display.

findings.label: Chip
findings.note: From Apple's US spec page. No price was shown in the page text.

findings.label: External displays supported
findings.value: 1 external display, up to native 4K at 60 Hz, alongside the built-in display at full native resolution
findings.note: Apple: 'Supports one external display with up to a native resolution of 4K at 60Hz'. A two-screen extender on native video can therefore extend only one added screen.

findings.label: Video-capable USB-C ports
findings.value: 1 of 2: the USB 3 (USB-C) port supports charging, DisplayPort (native DP 1.4, HBR3) and USB 3 at 10 Gb/s; the USB 2 (USB-C) port supports charging and USB 2 (480 Mb/s) only, with no DisplayPort listed
findings.note: Apple's image captions place both USB-C ports on the left side and the 3.5 mm jack on the right. A single-cable USB-C extender plugged into the USB 2 port gets no native video.

findings.label: Port Apple says to use for a display, and stated exclusion
findings.value: Connect a hub or display to the USB 3 port ('the left port'); 'Devices that use only Thunderbolt aren't compatible with MacBook Neo.'
findings.note: Apple's troubleshooting aside for accessories that don't work. The fetched text did not explain why it calls the USB 3 port 'the left port' when both ports are on the left side.

findings.label: Display size and weight
findings.note: This matters for lid fit against an extender's stated laptop-size range.

findings.label: External displays supported
findings.value: Up to 2 external displays (two up to 6K 60 Hz or 4K 144 Hz; or one up to 8K 60 Hz / 5K 120 Hz / 4K 240 Hz); 'up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port'
findings.source_title: MacBook Air 13- and 15-inch with M5 - Tech Specs - Apple
findings.note: The figures are the same for the 13-inch and 15-inch models. Apple's page does not mention any lid-open or lid-closed condition.

findings.label: Video-capable ports
findings.value: 2 Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, each with charging, DisplayPort (native DP 1.4, HBR3, DSC), Thunderbolt 4 and USB 4 at 40 Gb/s; plus MagSafe 3
findings.source_title: MacBook Air 13- and 15-inch with M5 - Tech Specs - Apple
findings.note: Two video-capable ports means a dual extender can run one native cable per screen without a driver.

findings.label: Mac compatibility (reviewer)
findings.value: Macworld: plain (non-Pro/Max) M1 and M2 Macs and the MacBook Neo connect a single monitor and need Mobile Pixels' free software to run the Trio 3 Pro; compatible with 13–16-inch MacBooks
findings.source_title: Best Portable Monitors for Mac 2026 | Macworld
findings.note: Named reviewer statement. Macworld also writes that the software is 'rather like DisplayLink'.

findings.label: Driver and OS (maker FAQ)
findings.value: Chromebook: 'No driver needed for any Chrome laptop'; Mac: OS above 10.12; on Windows the USB-A connection uses a DisplayLink driver
findings.note: The FAQ does not name a USB-C Alt Mode requirement or mention the MacBook Neo. It says several Duex units can run 'as long as you have enough ports'.

findings.label: Variants and connection (maker store listing)
findings.value: Duex Plus DS 13.3-inch or Duex Max DS 14.1-inch; USB-C and Mini HDMI inputs 'without the need for drivers or software'; store listing from-price $183.99 (compare-at $299.99), in stock
findings.note: Read through storecheck search of mobilepixels.us. The search does not say which variant the from-price belongs to. The product page itself returned HTTP 429, so I could not read prices for each variant.

findings.label: Laptop fit (reviewer guidance)
findings.value: iTechGuides: Duex Max DS for laptops 'roughly 14 inches or larger'; Duex Plus DS suits 'many 13- to 14-inch laptops'
findings.note: This is the reviewer's guidance, not the maker's range. On that guidance the 13.0-inch Neo is closer to the Plus DS.
